summary: The format of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, network and host parts, subnet masks, how an address is assigned to a device, and public versus private addresses.

theory.title: Format of an IP address and how it is assigned

blocks.title: IPv6
rows: 8 groups of 4 hex digits separated by colons: `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329`
Leading zeros dropped and one run of zero groups written `::` → `2001:db8::ff00:42:8329`
IPv4 addresses ran out; IPv6 gives 2¹²⁸ addresses, simpler headers, built-in security

blocks.text: Network part, host part and the subnet mask

blocks.content: An IP address has a **network ID** (which network) and a **host ID** (which device on that network). The **subnet mask** shows which bits are which: 1-bits = network, 0-bits = host.

blocks.title: 188.10.52.2 with mask 255.255.0.0
blocks.content:
- Mask 255.255.0.0 → first **two** octets are the network.
- Network address: **188.10.0.0**
- Host part: **0.0.52.2**
- First octet 188 is in 128–191 → **class B**.

blocks.text: How a device gets an IP address

items.title: Dynamic (DHCP)
items.content: A **DHCP server** (often the router) automatically **leases** an address from a pool when the device joins the network; it may change next time.

items.title: Static
items.content: The address is **set manually** and does not change. Used for **servers, printers, routers** that others must always find at the same address.

blocks.title: DHCP in brief
items: The device broadcasts "I need an address" (**Discover**).
The DHCP server **offers** a free address.
The device **requests** it; the server **acknowledges** and records the lease (with the subnet mask, gateway and DNS server).

rows: A **local network** only — reused in millions of LANs
The local router (DHCP) or the administrator

blocks.title: NAT (Network Address Translation)
blocks.content: The router has **one public address** and gives devices private addresses. It **translates** between them, so many devices share one public IP.

blocks.title: Implications for security
rows: Devices are **hidden** behind the router/NAT — attackers on the Internet cannot connect to them directly
Devices are **directly reachable** — open to scanning and attacks; need a firewall and updates
Outgoing connections are still possible, so malware can still "call home"
Servers need public addresses but should expose only required ports
